name: The Associates
label: Beggars Banquet
lede: Alan Rankine and Billy Mackenzie wrote "Party Fears Two" on a hungover Sunday in 1977, sat on it for five years, then took it onto Top of the Pops with a banjo, a beret and a voice nobody else in British pop could touch.

hero.by: Billy Mackenzie at Dundee University, 1985. Wikimedia Commons

eras.title: "I've got to have that voice"
eras.text: A Linlithgow guitarist playing chicken-in-a-basket lounges heard a Dundee singer in an Edinburgh ballroom and poached him. Three years and several band names later, they got noticed by covering a David Bowie single while it was still in the charts.

q: I've got to have that voice. I need to meet that person.
years.src: The Guardian: Alan Rankine obituary · Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Rankine hears Billy Mackenzie at Tiffany's in Edinburgh
years.p: [[Alan Rankine|9e8a2828-33ac-4622-9041-dfef405c28f4]] needs a singer for Caspian, a covers band working miners' welfare clubs. Mackenzie is on stage with a cod-funk act, and Rankine lures him away.
years.xp:
Mackenzie couldn't stand Caspian's straight, testosterone-heavy line-up, so he and Rankine started writing and playing as a duo. Rankine invited him to stay at his girlfriend's flat in Linlithgow.

Early names included the Ascorbic Ones, which Rankine later called a fantasy band they invented to give themselves a past, the Mike Lawrence Quintet and Mental Torture.

years.src: Classic Pop · The Guardian: Alan Rankine obituary
years.h: A hungover Sunday at the piano produces "Party Fears Two"
years.p: In Rankine's parents' lounge in Linlithgow, the melody arrives out of nowhere. At punk's height it feels unreleasable, so they put it away.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Associates · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie
years.h: An unauthorised "Boys Keep Swinging", weeks after Bowie's
years.p: Released without permission six weeks after Bowie's version hit the UK top 10, on the duo's own Double-Hip label. MCA picks it up and John Peel plays it.
years.xp: Mackenzie said the point was to provoke: "People said, 'That is awful. How dare they!'" It worked: the attention brought a deal with Chris Parry's Fiction Records, home of [[The Cure|69ee3720-a7cb-4402-b48d-a02c366f2bcf]].

eras.title: The year of singles
eras.text: A debut on Fiction, a borrowed Cure bassist and a rent-paid flat they got thrown out of. Then the Associates moved to Beggars Banquet's Situation Two imprint and made a string of singles so strange that even 1981 couldn't place them.

years.src: Classic Pop · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: The Affectionate Punch, co-produced by Mike Hedges
years.p: Critics compare it to [[Joy Division|9a58fda3-f4ed-4080-a3a5-f457aac9fcdd]] and the Cure. The live rhythm section, [[Michael Dempsey|e1fcd5e6-99e8-43f5-badc-4001cd299872]] and John Murphy, isn't on it.
years.xp: [[Mike Hedges|5b907598-26a5-4ad6-bfba-1a32a065e1ff]], who'd engineered the Cure, once tried to record drums underwater. "He could play a piano stool and make it sound good," Hedges said of Rankine.

years.src: Classic Pop · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie
years.h: The Cure's bassist joins, and a fish tank costs them the flat
years.p: Touring with [[The Cure|69ee3720-a7cb-4402-b48d-a02c366f2bcf]], they recruit Cure founder Dempsey on bass and Australian drummer Murphy. Parry pays their rent at 52 Carlton Hill, St John's Wood, until a leaking fish tank gets them evicted.

years.src: Classic Pop
years.h: "Q Quarters" costs £100, then speed puts them in hospital
years.p: Cut overnight with Flood at Morgan Studios. A bad night on seven grams of speed leaves both men on heart monitors for four days, Rankine says.
years.xp: The Morgan sessions ran from 9pm Sunday to 9am Monday. "We had Rick Wakeman banging on the door trying to get into his Monday morning session," Rankine told Classic Pop.

years.cap: The Associates as a four-piece, Mackenzie and Rankine with bandmates, c. 1981
years.src: Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Mackenzie sings "Kitchen Person" down a vacuum cleaner tube
years.p: Back with Hedges at his Playground Studios, an electric typewriter joins the rhythm section. Melody Maker makes it Single of the Week.

years.src: Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Fourth Drawer Down gathers the Situation Two singles
years.p: "Tell Me Easter's on Friday", "Kitchen Person", "White Car in Germany": singles too odd for 1981 radio, collected on Beggars Banquet's indie imprint.
years.xp: For "White Car in Germany" Mackenzie sang through greaseproof paper and a comb over flapping hardboard. "Ours got peeled off halfway through," he said of the chart, as "Vienna" and "Tainted Love" sold. "That would soon change."

eras.title: Six months at the centre of pop
eras.text: A Beggars Banquet deal through Warner paid for a Camden studio full of new toys, and the Associates spent it all on Sulk. For half a year they were everywhere. Then Mackenzie wouldn't tour, and Rankine walked.

years.cap: Mackenzie and Rankine in the Sulk press kit, 1982
years.src: Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Half the £60,000 advance goes straight to Mike Hedges
years.p: Demos of "Party Fears Two" and "Club Country" land a deal with Beggars Banquet via Warner. Hedges builds Playground Studios on Camden's Bayham Street, with a Harrison console.
years.xp: Beggars had a licensing deal with WEA at the time, mainly for [[Gary Numan|6cb79cb2-9087-44d4-828b-5c6fdff2c957]], so the Associates went out on their own Associates imprint through Warner. Rankine played most of the instruments on Sulk; the Cure left a mountain of beer cans when they sublet the studio.

years.src: Classic Pop · The Guardian: Alan Rankine obituary · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie
yt: 'Party Fears Two' on Top of the Pops
years.h: "Party Fears Two" on Top of the Pops: a beret, a banjo, a fencing suit
years.p: Mackenzie in a belted raincoat, Rankine with chopsticks in his hair and Samurai make-up. The single reaches No. 9 in March.

years.src: Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Murphy is out after Mackenzie overhears a phone call
years.p: Mackenzie heard drummer John Murphy grumbling about the pop band he played in. Steve Goulding takes the drums; Martha and the Muffins' [[Martha Ladly|df12ddd4-26c0-496a-a008-55426c59698c]] adds keys and backing vocals.

years.src: Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Sulk, "ABBA meets Bet Lynch on acid"
years.p: Mackenzie's description. It goes top 10, "Club Country" reaches No. 13, and Melody Maker names it album of the year.
years.xp:
Peter Ashworth shot the cover in a South London conservatory lit through blue and green gels; it now hangs in the National Portrait Gallery. Mackenzie gave Hedges instructions like making a sound "like grass, Egypt or coming from inside a sarcophagus".

After the final mix Rankine burst into tears: "a release of nervous tension."

years.cap: Mackenzie and Rankine in Japan's Music Life, September 1982
years.src: Classic Pop
years.h: Two chocolate guitars from Harrods for "18 Carat Love Affair"
years.p: A spare in case the first melted under the lights. Rankine fed the remains to the audience, and they glued DJ Dave Lee Travis's dressing room doors shut.
years.xp: Travis had slagged them off on the radio, Rankine said. The single stalled at No. 21. "Billy was very upset about that," Hedges said.

years.src: The Guardian: Alan Rankine obituary · Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Mackenzie cancels the tour and turns down Sire; Rankine quits
years.p: Mackenzie in 1985. He called off the tour the night before the Edinburgh opener, then declined [[Seymour Stein|3a95e565-673e-430b-abb4-e17229320fdf]]'s offer of America at Langan's Brasserie.
years.xp:
The Guardian says Mackenzie balked at eight months touring Sulk in the US. "He hated touring. Hated the repetition of miming songs," Rankine said. Sessions booked at Compass Point in the Bahamas were cancelled.

Rankine spent four months drinking and brooding, then produced the [[Cocteau Twins|000fc734-b7e1-4a01-92d1-f544261b43f5]] and went solo.

eras.title: One voice, one name
eras.text: Mackenzie kept the Associates name and the label kept losing patience. There were hits with Yello and Shirley Bassey, a lot of whippets, and an album Warner refused to put out.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Associates · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie
years.h: Perhaps sells about 40,000 and leaves Mackenzie in debt to Warner
years.p: Made with guitarist Steve Reid and producer Martin Rushent. It peaks at No. 23; "Breakfast" is the last top 50 hit.
years.xp: Afterwards Mackenzie retreated to Dundee and his favourite hobby, breeding racing whippets, according to the Independent.

years.src: Wikipedia: Billy MacKenzie · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Mackenzie writes "The Rhythm Divine" for Yello, and Shirley Bassey sings it
years.p: He writes lyrics for two songs on Yello's One Second and sings "Moon on Ice" himself. His own version of "The Rhythm Divine" turns up later.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Associates · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie
years.h: Warner shelves The Glamour Chase; a 3D "Heart of Glass" comes out
years.p: WEA calls the album commercially unviable. The Blondie cover, with a 3D sleeve and glasses, reaches No. 56 and ends his time with the label.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Wild and Lonely, the last record called Associates
years.p: Released on Virgin's Circa label and produced by Julian Mendelsohn, it reaches No. 71. From here Mackenzie records under his own name.

eras.title: The reunion that didn't, and the elegies
eras.text: Rankine and Mackenzie wrote a dozen songs together in 1993 and still couldn't agree about the road. Four years later Mackenzie was dead, and the people he'd sung with started writing songs about him.

years.src: The Guardian: Alan Rankine obituary · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Rankine and Mackenzie reunite, write a dozen songs, and stop
years.p: The demos were promising and the press got excited, but Mackenzie still wouldn't tour. He could fly to New York and play to 4,000 fans in one night, the Guardian notes.
years.xp: Rankine went on to lecture at Stow College in Glasgow, where he helped found the student label Electric Honey, which worked with [[Belle and Sebastian|e5c7b94f-e264-473c-bb0f-37c85d4d5c70]], [[Biffy Clyro|892500b7-09a6-4049-ba92-2d192dd70563]] and Snow Patrol.

years.src: Wikipedia: Billy MacKenzie · The Independent: Obituary: Billy MacKenzie · Classic Pop
years.h: Billy Mackenzie dies in Auchterhouse, aged 39
years.p: Mackenzie died by suicide, overdosing on paracetamol and prescription medication in a shed in his father's garden, shortly after his mother's death. Wikipedia says he had clinical depression.
years.xp: He had just signed to Nude Records and was planning a comeback with new songs written with Steve Aungle; Beyond the Sun came out later that year. Siouxsie Sioux wrote the Creatures' "Say" about a meeting they'd planned, and [[Robert Smith|7d1a1624-784b-4f89-8ff9-b9b493cd059d]] wrote the Cure's "Cut Here" about brushing him off backstage weeks before.

years.src: The Guardian: Alan Rankine obituary · Wikipedia: The Associates
years.h: Alan Rankine dies at 64
years.p: Ladytron's tribute: "No Associates = No Ladytron." He had been planning a book.

sources.title: Classic Pop: The Associates, 'We were firing on all cylinders at the speed of light'
